specAnchors.text: understand how selective breeding can develop plants with desired characteristics

primer.text: Plant breeders run the same choosing game as animal breeders, but on crops. This note defines artificial selection in plants, tours the features growers chase — from disease resistance to flower size — and then examines the hidden cost: repeatedly breeding the best-related plants narrows the gene pool and leaves a crop exposed.

modules.title: Defining the Process and Its Crop Targets
modules.opening: Artificial selection in plants means people, not the environment, pick the parents: individuals showing a wanted feature are crossed, their offspring are screened, and only offspring displaying the feature are crossed again. Growers chase disease resistance in food crops, bigger harvests, tolerance of drought or harsh weather, improved fruit flavour and larger or more striking flowers. One wild ancestor can even be sculpted into several entirely different vegetables.
keyPoints: Selective breeding in plants starts by crossing individuals that show a desirable feature.
Because not every seedling expresses the feature, offspring that do are chosen and re-crossed.
Many generations of this screening pass before a new variety reliably shows the feature.
Grower targets include disease resistance, higher yield, weather hardiness, better flavour and larger or unusual flowers.
Wild brassica was moulded by breeders into cauliflower, cabbage and broccoli, plus Brussels sprouts, kale and kohlrabi — six crops from one ancestor.

low.restatement: Cross the best plants, keep the seedlings that show the trait, cross again — many rounds until the crop is reliable.
low.analogy: Like picking only the fastest sprinters for relay training each season — after several seasons every runner on the team is fast.
low.examPointer: Name the loop: select, cross, select offspring, repeat — then quote at least two grower targets.

medium.restatement: Each generation, plants expressing the target characteristic are intercrossed while the remainder are discarded, so the alleles behind the trait rise in frequency until the variety breeds reliably.
medium.analogy: A seed catalogue that gets narrower every year: each reprint keeps only the pages gardeners actually order, until the catalogue is exactly what buyers want.
medium.examPointer: Anchor Higher-tier answers in allele language: selection raises the frequency of the desired alleles across the generations.

modules.title: Inbreeding and the Shrinking Gene Pool
modules.opening: Chasing the 'best' individuals has a catch: the top performers are often close relatives, so pairing them is inbreeding. Each round of inbreeding trims the variety of alleles held by the population — the gene pool narrows. A narrowed pool raises the odds that a lineage inherits harmful defects and leaves it poorly armed against new diseases, because fewer resistant alleles remain in circulation.
keyPoints: Inbreeding means mating closely related 'best' individuals generation after generation.
The gene pool shrinks — the population holds fewer different alleles.
A reduced pool raises the chance of harmful genetic defects being inherited.
It also raises vulnerability to new disease, because resistant alleles are less likely to be present.

low.restatement: Breed only relatives, the gene pool shrinks, and defects plus disease risk climb.
low.analogy: A choir that recruits only from one family: everyone shares the same weaknesses, and one virus could silence the whole choir.
low.examPointer: Link the chain explicitly: inbreeding to smaller gene pool to more defects and less disease resistance.

medium.restatement: Restricting matings to related high performers removes allele variants from the population; with fewer alternatives, inheriting damaging recessives becomes more likely and resistance alleles spread less.
medium.analogy: An investment portfolio built only from one company's shares: any bad news about that company sinks everything, with nothing different to absorb the shock.
medium.examPointer: Quote the two consequences separately — inherited defects and disease vulnerability — for full marks.

glossary.definition: Human choice of which plants cross, directing the features of the next generation.
A plant line produced by selection that reliably shows the chosen feature.
The full set of different alleles carried by the individuals in a population.
One version of a gene; different alleles give different forms of a feature.
Repeated mating of closely related individuals, which narrows the gene pool.
